clue.text: Defend gagster, outspoken figure

parts.note: a stand-up is a comedian who tells gags on stage

indicators.note: something outspoken is spoken out, so the word wanted is the one heard rather than the one written

parts.note: a figure is a numeral, here the one after three

explanation.surface: A public figure speaks up to defend a comedian in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' looks like a person speaking out, but it is a number; said out loud it matches the little preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand up for someone is an idiom meaning to support them openly against attack.

clue.text: Is a crossword compiler caught leaving schools?

definitions.note: Read as describing what a compiler does: one who is a crossword setter sets puzzles, so the phrase stands for the verb.

indicators.note: to leave is to depart, so this letter goes out of the word it sat in

parts.note: schools of thought or religion are sects
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A puzzle-setter is caught playing truant from school.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a setter caught skipping lessons; in fact the opening words are the definition, since what a setter does is set.
explanation.definitionFit: A compiler's job is producing puzzles, and the verb for producing them is what the setter does.

clue.text: Axe a finale from Wagner, like The Ring

parts.note: to axe a plan or law is to cancel it
taken as written

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so only the word's last character is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of the composer's name

explanation.surface: A critic proposes cutting the ending of Wagner's Ring cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ring sounds like Wagner's opera cycle, and the composer's name sits beside it, but the definition just means ring-shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: Annular is the adjective for circular band shapes, from the Latin annulus, a little circle.

clue.text: I follow the units of police — and I'm terribly tense!

indicators.note: done terribly means done badly, so the surrounding letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A rookie tags along behind police squads and confesses to nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Units' suggests squads of officers, but in arithmetic the units are the ones column, and the dot after it is speaking in the first person.
explanation.definitionFit: In a written number the dot sits immediately after the ones column, separating whole numbers from fractions.

clue.text: Film-maker supporting fascist regime's leader

parts.note: pro means in favour of
Il Duce was Mussolini's title as Italy's fascist dictator

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening character of the word is used

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A movie director props up the head of a fascist state.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a propagandist; the pieces are a word for 'in favour', Mussolini's title, and a single initial.
explanation.definitionFit: A producer is the person who finances and oversees the making of a movie.

clue.text: Rancid butter firmly grasped

parts.note: food that has gone off is rancid or spoiled
a pat is a small slab of butter

explanation.surface: Someone gripped a lump of rancid butter tightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rancid butter' reads as one phrase, but the two words give separate pieces; 'firmly grasped' means learnt thoroughly, not physically held.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowing something thus means having memorised it perfectly, an idiom for a mental grip rather than a physical one.

clue.text: Might one cram whiskey into boozer?

definitions.note: Phrased as a question about a person who might cram, it stands for the noun naming that person.

indicators.note: putting something into another thing places it inside

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard
W is whiskey in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone wonders about stuffing whisky into the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a boozer is a pub, which suits the whiskey, but here it is the drinker. Swot is British slang for a pupil who studies hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A studious pupil who revises intensively before exams does exactly what cramming means.

clue.text: Holiday with e.g. successful film star

parts.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with
a successful film is one example of a hit
the Sun is our nearest star

explanation.surface: A film star goes on holiday after a box-office success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film star' reads as a celebrity, but the words split: the film is a box-office success and the star is the one in our sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The week around Whit Sunday, or Pentecost, was a traditional British public holiday period.

clue.text: Grand tours south of Spain's capital maybe booming

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all round it, so one piece travels around another

parts.note: a thou is slang for a thousand, and a grand is a thousand pounds or dollars
south of means below, or beneath

indicators.note: a capital letter begins a word, and 'maybe' admits the city is not meant, so take the first character only

parts.note: the first letter of the country's name

explanation.surface: Grand tours of southern Spain may be loud affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand tours' suggests travel, but grand is slang for a thousand, and 'south of' is simply a word meaning below rather than a placing instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Booming describes a deep, very loud resounding noise like a storm's rumble overhead.

clue.text: Bracing tête-à-tête, say, about student teacher's method

parts.note: a tonic is something invigorating, as a bracing walk is

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: a tête-à-tête is an S-shaped two-seater settee, one example of the furniture
L for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: A brisk heart-to-heart with a pupil explains a teacher's approach.
explanation.walkthrough: Tête-à-tête looks like a private chat, but it also names a two-seater settee. Tonic sol-fa is the do-re-mi system for teaching singing.
explanation.definitionFit: This system of syllables for musical notes was devised in Victorian Britain for teaching sight-singing in schools.

clue.text: Place in which soldier evicts tenant

indicators.note: to evict is to throw out an occupant, so those letters are removed

parts.note: an army officer rank just below captain
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A soldier throws a lodger out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The officer's rank literally houses a tenant at its end; throwing that occupant out leaves the French word for place, as in 'in lieu of'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French borrowing survives in English mainly in the phrase meaning instead of, literally in the place of.

clue.text: Flattening what could be a female medic's gown?

parts.note: making a surface level is evening it out
DR is doctor and -ESS is the feminine suffix, as in actress

explanation.surface: Someone irons out a woman doctor's gown.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests pressing a surgeon's gown; a doctor's title plus the feminine ending makes a jokey coinage, hence 'what could be'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a long formal frock worn by women to dinners, balls and other formal occasions.

clue.text: Brief recession where people have little money

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the word loses its final character

parts.note: a slump is an economic downturn

explanation.surface: A short downturn leaves people poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief recession' reads as a short economic dip, which fits the poverty theme; the adjective actually shortens the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a squalid, overcrowded district inhabited by very poor residents.

clue.text: Adult in nude vids developed rash

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another
something developed has been worked into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
A is the film-certificate abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: Making explicit home videos was an ill-judged move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Developed' suggests processing film, which suits the videos, but it signals reworking the letters. Unadvised is an older word for ill-considered.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting without due thought or counsel is reckless and imprudent, so the two words overlap in meaning.

clue.text: Funny nurses working with drug initially, tending to husband

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so this piece goes at the front

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, cradling something within

parts.note: comical means funny
on means working, as a switched-on machine is

explanation.surface: Amusing nurses on duty hand out medicine while caring for a husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' looks like the people, but it is the verb for holding; 'husband' is the old verb meaning to manage resources carefully, not a spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: To husband resources is to use them sparingly, and being thrifty in that way is the adjective here.

clue.text: Singer in clubs given a wave

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
taken as written
a roller is a long heavy sea wave

explanation.surface: A nightclub singer gets waved at by the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs suggests nightclubs, but it is the card suit, abbreviated as in bridge notation.
explanation.definitionFit: This is someone who sings Christmas songs, often going door to door in a group.

clue.text: More vacuous monarch succeeds Anne I, curiously

indicators.note: to succeed is to follow on afterwards, so this piece is placed at the end
curiously means in a strange way, so the letters arrive in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written
R for rex or regina, king or queen

explanation.surface: An even emptier-headed king follows Queen Anne onto the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a royal succession, and Anne was indeed followed by a king; the numeral I is just a letter for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means silly or devoid of sense, and the comparative form means more so.

clue.text: Gradually withdraw shape, it's suggested

parts.note: the letters of this word rearranged
the answer's second word read as a rearranging signal, so the answer itself suggests the clue word

explanation.surface: A tip for slowly retiring something, hinting at its form.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: read the answer as wordplay, and PHASE 'out' is a jumble of PHASE, which gives the clue word shape.
explanation.definitionFit: To phase out a product or policy is to withdraw it in stages rather than all at once.

clue.text: Out to seize ring that's fancy

indicators.note: to seize is to grab hold of, so one piece clutches another inside it

parts.note: not in means out, as of a person away from home
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A thief goes out to snatch an elegant ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an adjective for the ring, but it is the noun for a whim or idea.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy in the sense of a whim or passing idea is an impression held in the mind.

clue.text: Little perch, perhaps, one seen in a pond

parts.note: a tad is a small amount
a perch is an old unit of length, also called a rod; 'perhaps' flags the equivalence

explanation.surface: A small fish, maybe one swimming in a pond.
explanation.walkthrough: Perch looks like the fish, which suits the pond, but it is the old measure of length, five and a half yards.
explanation.definitionFit: Frog larvae hatch and grow in ponds, so they are among the creatures commonly found in garden water.

clue.text: I appreciate that French solver carries cloth round

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so one piece holds the rest within it

parts.note: the solver is always 'you', and tu is the French for you
a hanky is a handkerchief, a small square of cloth
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Thanks are due to a French puzzler who brings round a cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French solver' is a crossword in-joke: the solver is always addressed as 'you', so in French it is the familiar pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying the phrase expresses gratitude, which is what a speaker who values something says.

clue.text: Does one long period end in autumn? Let me think

definitions.note: Read as 'one who does long', a person who longs; the verb phrase stands for the noun.

parts.note: a year is a period of time

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final character, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the season
er is the hesitation noise of someone thinking

explanation.surface: Someone ponders whether a long stretch of time finishes in autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: The question sounds like a calendar puzzle, but its opening words define the answer, read as one who does long for something.
explanation.definitionFit: This noun names a person who pines or hankers after something, formed from the verb yearn.

clue.text: Project number five needs right cutting tool

parts.note: a project is a scheme or plan
E is the fifth letter of the alphabet
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Project five on the list requires the correct cutting tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Project number five' reads as a work item on a list; split it into a scheme, then the fifth letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: This woodworking machine or hand tool shaves timber smooth by slicing off thin layers.

clue.text: Chain hosts wrapped around duck

indicators.note: wrapping something means enclosing it, so one piece encases the other

parts.note: MCs, masters of ceremonies, host events
Donald Duck is the Disney cartoon character

explanation.surface: Fast-food staff serve duck in a wrap.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a fast-food wrap; the hosts are compères, and the duck is Disney's.
explanation.definitionFit: The global fast-food restaurant brand runs thousands of branches worldwide, making it a chain.

clue.text: Kid from the east eating hot curry

indicators.note: reading from the east in an across entry means right to left, back to front
eating takes something inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a lad is a boy or kid
H for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A child from the Orient tucks into a spicy curry.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the Indian lentil dish, also spelt dal.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiced lentil stew from South Asia is commonly counted among curries on restaurant menus.

clue.text: Electronic current blocker somewhere in Holland

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
a dam blocks a current of water

explanation.surface: An electronic device blocks the current in a Dutch town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' suggests electricity after 'Electronic', but it is a flow of water.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheese takes its name from a small town north of Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

clue.text: Prune one's cultivated in field

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to cut back or trim short
second meaning: a plant grown in quantity on farmland

explanation.surface: A dried plum is grown out in the field.
explanation.walkthrough: Prune reads as the dried fruit, which sits well with cultivation, but it is the verb for cutting back.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb for trimming short and as a noun for plants harvested from farmland.

clue.text: Lacking control, Cockney suffering after drinking with Scottish hooligan

indicators.note: Cockney speech drops initial aitches, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: suffering the morning after heavy drinking
ned is Scottish slang for a young hooligan

explanation.surface: A rowdy London drinker teams up with a Glasgow thug, both out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner, and dropping the aitch is the classic sign of that accent.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without rule or authority over it is unrestrained, running wild.

clue.text: A number of Germans weren't trustworthy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a German art song

explanation.surface: Several Germans proved unreliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A number' reads as a quantity of people, but a number is a song; a Lied is the German art song of Schubert and Schumann.
explanation.definitionFit: German for song names the nineteenth-century art song, and the same letters are the past tense of telling falsehoods.

clue.text: Set out to pen holy book, with odd barrier to fiction?

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so one piece holds another
out suggests letters knocked out of place, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
Ruth is a book of the Old Testament
rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: Someone plans to write a scripture with a curious barrier against fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' reads as a phrasal verb meaning to plan, but the two words split into fodder and signal. The definition is playful: a drug that forces honesty bars invention.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug supposedly compelling honest answers prevents lies, which are fictions, so it stops them.
